results.title: Translating Trauma-Informed Principles into Trauma-Responsive Practices - Institute for Child and Family Well-Being
results.content: Building on the work of Harris and Fallot5 and other seminal contributions, the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) issued six TIC principles that guide service agencies in recognizing and responding to trauma.6. In response, scholars have started to outline how TIC principles manifest as practice elements such as screening, assessment, and referral to treatment.7 As a prime example, **Trauma Screening, Brief Intervention and Referral to Treatment** (T-SBIRT) is a 10-minute protocol that aims to increase access to mental health services.8 Due to its brevity and uncomplicated design, T-SBIRT can readily be implemented by general practitioners in many service settings. Whereas TIC practices focus on promoting client engagement and can be implemented by a broad class of general practitioners, trauma-focused treatment should be provided by highly trained specialists. Although the boundaries between TIC and trauma-focused treatment are becoming clearer, there is a need to understand what differences there are, if any, between trauma-informed and trauma-sensitive services. Thus, a trauma-sensitive approach would be appropriate for systems and organizations where all trauma-focused and many trauma-informed approaches are beyond the scope of practice for most staff, but where greater awareness of trauma and certain TIC applications can still enhance the services that staff provide. Teachers who are aware of the signs and symptoms of trauma also can help to link children to school-based mental health staff who are properly trained to implement TIC practices such as screening, assessment, and referral to treatment. Evidence-based TIC practices such as screening, assessment, and referral can also help to increase access to trauma-focused treatments and other interventions that foster resilience and recovery. Policy and system changes are also needed to increase access to trauma-focused, trauma-informed, and trauma-sensitive services that enhance the health and well-being of individuals, families, and communities — especially those who are at the greatest risk of trauma and its consequences. results.title: Best Practices for Writing Informed Consent Forms in Clinical Research
results.content: # Best Practices for Writing Informed Consent Forms in Clinical Research. Informed consent forms (ICFs) are a crucial aspect of clinical research, ensuring that participants are fully informed about the study they are considering, including its purpose, procedures, risks, and benefits. Ethical clinical research requires participants to understand these elements before they agree to take part in a study. In this blog, we’ll outline the best practices for writing informed consent forms in clinical research to ensure clarity, compliance, and participant understanding. One of the most important considerations in writing an informed consent form is ensuring that the language is clear and understandable to the average person. For example, instead of writing “The investigational drug will be administered to participants,” you can say “You will receive the study drug during the trial.”. One of the central functions of an informed consent form is to ensure that participants are fully aware of any potential risks and benefits associated with the study.

results.title: Informed Consent in Research: A Comprehensive Guide
results.content:
Title: Informed Consent in Research: A Comprehensive Guide
Informed consent is a fundamental ethical principle in research that ensures participants are fully aware of what they're agreeing to when they take part in a study. 5. **Documentation**: While not always required, documenting the informed consent process is crucial for most research studies. 3. **Transparency and Trust**: By providing full disclosure, informed consent builds trust between researchers and participants, which is crucial for the integrity of the research process. 2. **Beneficence**: By fully disclosing potential risks and benefits, informed consent helps ensure that the well-being of participants is prioritized over research objectives. Let's explore the key steps involved in obtaining informed consent, ensuring that participants are fully aware of what they're agreeing to and that researchers are meeting their ethical and legal obligations. By following these steps and considerations, researchers can ensure that their informed consent process is thorough, ethical, and respectful of participants' autonomy. By following these best practices, researchers can create consent documents that not only meet ethical and legal requirements but also truly inform and empower potential participants. 3. **Online research**: For some web-based studies, the act of clicking through to participate after reading an information sheet can be considered implied consent. By understanding and appropriately implementing these alternatives to written informed consent, researchers can conduct ethical studies while adapting to diverse research contexts and participant needs. In research, informed consent is a process by which a participant voluntarily confirms their willingness to participate in a study after being informed of all aspects relevant to their decision. * Informed consent is a cornerstone of ethical research, ensuring participant autonomy and protection. * **What is informed consent in research?** Informed consent is a process where participants voluntarily agree to take part in a study after being fully informed about its purpose, procedures, risks, and benefits. * **Why is informed consent important?** It protects participants' rights, ensures ethical conduct of research, builds trust, and helps maintain the integrity of scientific studies. * **How can researchers ensure participants understand the consent information?** Use clear, jargon-free language, provide information in the participant's preferred language, and assess comprehension through questions or teach-back methods.
